procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Cuttack-Dhenkanal, Cuttack, in Sessions Trial No. 9-C of 1950.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 19th September, 1950, of the Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Cuttack-Dhenkanal, Cuttack, in Sessions Trial No. 9-C of 1950.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Orissa at Cuttack heard Criminal Appeal No. 66 of 1950 arising out of the Sessions Court's judgment and order. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The accused then applied for a certificate to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 134(1)(c). The High Court granted leave to appeal on all three points raised by the accused, considering the first point to be of importance, even though it found two of the points to be of insufficient importance to justify a certificate.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court granted a certificate to appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sanction for prosecution is invalid if the facts constituting the offence are not detailed on the face of the sanction itself.

facts: The sanction for prosecution in this case was general and did not specify the particular facts constituting the alleged offence on its face.
law: A sanction for prosecution is not required to be in any particular form or even in writing.
It is not essential for the validity of a sanction that the facts constituting the offence be detailed on the face of the sanction document itself, although it is desirable.
An omission to set out the facts on the sanction is not a fatal defect.
application: The Court held that if the facts are not present on the face of the sanction, the prosecution bears the burden of proving through other evidence (extraneous evidence or 'aliunde') that the sanctioning authority was aware of the facts constituting the offence when it granted the sanction.
As long as the prosecution can prove that the facts were placed before the sanctioning authority, the sanction is valid.
In this case, the Court noted that a letter from the District Magistrate to the sanctioning authority was sufficient proof that the relevant facts had been communicated.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court concluded that the sanction was not invalid. The failure to detail the facts on the face of the sanction is not a fatal error, provided the prosecution can prove through other means that the sanction was granted after the sanctioning authority was made aware of the facts of the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court was bound to presume the accused's guilt under section 5(3) once it was established that he possessed assets disproportionate to his known income and his explanation was found unsatisfactory.

facts: The accused, a Government Factory Inspector, was found in possession of Rs. 2,698 in cash.

The Court determined this amount was disproportionate to his known sources of income, which consisted of a salary of Rs. 450 a month and some travel allowances, especially considering his family expenses.
The accused provided an explanation for the money, but it was considered unsatisfactory and disbelieved by the lower courts.
law: Section 5(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act states that if an accused is found in possession of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to their known sources of income, for which they cannot provide a satisfactory account, the Court "shall presume" they are guilty of criminal misconduct.
The conviction can be based solely on this presumption.
application: The Supreme Court focused on the mandatory language of Section 5(3). It highlighted that the statute uses the word "shall presume," not "may presume."

This means that once the prosecution proves two things—(1) possession of assets disproportionate to known income and (2) that the accused's explanation is unsatisfactory—the court has no choice but to presume guilt.
In this case, the prosecution successfully established that the assets were disproportionate.
The lower courts had already determined, as a matter of fact, that the accused's explanation was unsatisfactory.
With these two conditions met, the Court found that Section 5(3) was automatically triggered.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that once it was established that the accused possessed assets disproportionate to his known income and his explanation was found unsatisfactory, the court was legally bound by the mandatory language of Section 5(3) ("shall presume") to presume his guilt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sanction for prosecution is invalid if the facts constituting the offence are not detailed on the face of the sanction itself.
appellant_arguments: The sanction was invalid because it lacked particulars of the offence.
The appellant relied on the Privy Council's judgment in Morarka's case to support the argument that the facts constituting the offence must be detailed.
respondent_arguments: The sanction was valid because the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(a) is of a general character and does not require individual acts of bribe-taking to be detailed.
The facts placed before the sanctioning authority, such as the information about bribe collection and the money found in his possession, were sufficient to validate the prosecution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court was bound to presume the accused's guilt under section 5(3) once it was established that he possessed assets disproportionate to his known income and his explanation was found unsatisfactory.
appellant_arguments: The appellant challenged the law regarding the presumption under section 5(3), suggesting that the court was not automatically bound to presume guilt and that other considerations should be taken into account.
respondent_arguments: Once the prosecution proves that the accused possesses disproportionate assets for which he cannot satisfactorily account, the court is legally bound to presume the accused is guilty.
The use of the word 'shall' in section 5(3) makes the presumption mandatory, not discretionary ('may').

cases.case_name: Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
cases.principle: A sanction for prosecution is not required to be in any particular form, or to set out the facts in respect of which it is given. An omission to set out the facts in the sanction is not fatal so long as the facts can be and are proved in some other way.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A sanction for prosecution is not required to be in any particular form, nor must it be in writing or set out the facts constituting the offense on its face. However, the prosecution carries the burden to prove that the sanction was given in respect of the specific facts constituting the offense charged. If the facts are not detailed on the sanction itself, the prosecution must prove through extraneous evidence that those facts were placed before the sanctioning authority.
obiter: It is desirable for the facts of the offense to be referred to on the face of the sanction to simplify the process of proof.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that a sanction for prosecution is not invalid merely because the facts constituting the offence are not detailed on its face, as long as it can be proven by other evidence that the relevant facts were placed before the sanctioning authority. Furthermore, once the prosecution establishes that an accused possesses assets disproportionate to their known income for which their explanation is unsatisfactory, the court is statutorily bound under section 5(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act to presume the accused is guilty of criminal misconduct, as the word 'shall' in the section makes the presumption mandatory.
legal_tests_applied: A sanction for prosecution is valid if the facts constituting the offence, though not set out in the sanction itself, are proven 'aliunde' (by other evidence) to have been placed before the sanctioning authority.

Under section 5(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, once the prosecution proves that an accused possesses pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income for which he cannot satisfactorily account, the court 'shall' presume the accused is guilty of criminal misconduct unless the contrary is proved.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the sanction was invalid for lacking particulars failed because the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(a) is of a general character and does not require individual acts of bribe-taking to be detailed. The omission of facts on the sanction itself is not a fatal defect so long as the facts can be proven in another way, which was done here through a letter (Exhibit 25) sent to the sanctioning authority.

The appellant's contention that the court was not bound to presume guilt was rejected because the plain language of section 5(3) uses the word 'shall', not 'may', making the presumption of guilt mandatory, not discretionary, once the factual predicate of disproportionate assets and an unsatisfactory explanation is met.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution successfully established the sanction's validity by proving that the facts on which the sanction was based, namely the information about bribe collection and the money found in the accused's possession, were placed before the sanctioning authority, even if not detailed on the sanction document itself.

The respondent's position that the presumption of guilt was mandatory was upheld because the court interpreted the word 'shall' in section 5(3) as imposing a legal obligation on the court to presume guilt once the prosecution proved the foundational facts of disproportionate assets and an unsatisfactory explanation from the accused.
